newsitem.title: USA: Ehrlich sees consumer sector adding to Q4 growth.
newsitem.headline: Ehrlich sees consumer sector adding to Q4 growth.

text.p: A senior U.S. Commerce Department official said on Monday the consumer sector would likely contribute positively to growth in the final quarter of this year, bringing growth in the period on par with the third quarter or slightly better.

"I think we're going to have a stronger Christmas than last year," U.S. Commerce Undersecretary Everett Ehrlich told Reuters. "I think the consumer is going to contribute positively to the fourth quarter."

Asked for his projections for fourth quarter growth, the Commerce official replied: "(It's) very early ... perhaps on par with the third quarter or maybe a little better, but that's very impressionistic."

The Commerce Department's preliminary estimate of gross domestic product growth showed the economy expanding at a moderate 2.0 percent pace in the third quarter, sharply less than the 4.7 percent surge recorded in the second quarter.
The department is scheduled to release its final estimate of third-quarter GDP on Dec. 20.
Concerning the fourth quarter, Ehrlich said the picture would become more clear with the release of additional data, such as the November retail sales report due out on Thursday.

While many analysts believe this year's holiday retail season will be an improvement over last year's lackluster performance, several have speculated that the heavy debt burdens carried by consumers might restrain spending.
Ehrlich, however, said many consumers are in a better position than might be suggested by the figures on debt, given the "wealth effect" from rising asset prices.
"Even if equity markets were to correct, the rate of growth in the value of households' assets is far in excess of the rate of growth of their debt," the U.S. official said.

Ehrlich said he saw strong underlying fundamentals in the U.S. economy, saying he believed it was possible to exceed the 2.0 percent growth rate of the third quarter without spurring higher inflation.
The major risk in the outlook right now, Ehrlich said, is not the domestic consumer sector but whether growth among the major U.S. trading partners will be begin to pick up.
On that subject, he said that the economies of both Canada and Mexico are improving and that there were prospects for improvement in Europe.
Ehrlich said there was also potential for improvement in Japan but that he was more cautious on the outlook there.
On balance, Erhlich saw prospects for an improved U.S. trade deficit.
Turning to the subject of an independent commission's report last week on the Consumer Price Index, Ehrlich said, "It's a good first step. There is broad consensus that we mismeasure inflation."

The congressionally appointed commission led by Stanford University economist Michael Boskin estimated that the CPI overstates inflation by 1.1 percentage points a year. The CPI is published monthly by the Labor Department.

The panel said the problem with CPI was costing the federal government billions of dollars in lost tax revenues and overpayment of benefits such as Social Security because tax brackets and benefit programs are indexed to the CPI.
Ehrlich said the report from would be an important subject for discussion by the administration and the Congress.
He stressed that it is important to address measurement issues with the CPI but added that the issue should not be seen as a "veil" for action on the budget.

He also said there were some "conjectural issues" regarding estimates of the CPI's overstatement and that reaching a consensus on those issues would require "a broad discussion of all affected communities."
